title: Before the Budget: what workers look for
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Five questions that readers can ask when the Union Budget is presented.
body:
The Union Budget for 2026-27 is to be presented in Parliament on 1 February 2026. Headlines will talk about growth, the fiscal deficit and tax rates, but a working person can read the Budget in a more direct way: by asking whether it makes any difference to wages, jobs, pensions and security. This post offers a short guide for that kind of reading, based on what the Government has already announced, on the demands that BMS has put forward, and on how Budget documents are put together.

## What the Budget is, and why workers should read it

The Budget is the Government's statement of how it will raise and spend money in the coming year. Most of what the Government promises to workers, whether it is health cover for gig workers, an honorarium for Anganwadi workers or an incentive for hiring, has to be paid for from this statement. A law can create a right on paper, but a right needs funds, staff and systems to become real. That is why a union looks at the Budget as closely as it looks at a Code.

The Budget documents published on the official Budget website include the Finance Minister's speech, the Annual Financial Statement, the Demands for Grants of each ministry, an Output Outcome Framework for schemes, and a note on the implementation of the previous year's announcements. For a reader who wants to go beyond the speech, the last two are especially useful.

## Five simple questions

**1. Social security.** Is there provision for the gig, platform and unorganised workers' schemes under the Code on Social Security? The Code, which came into force on 21 November 2025, makes platform and gig workers eligible for social security for the first time, with aggregators contributing 1 to 2 per cent of their annual turnover, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay to such workers. In the Budget of 1 February 2025, the Finance Minister had announced identity cards and registration on the e-Shram portal for gig workers, with health cover under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, for nearly one crore workers. The question for 2026 is whether money and systems follow.

**2. Scheme workers.** Does the allocation for the Integrated Child Development Services, the National Health Mission and the PM POSHAN mid-day meal scheme allow an increase in honorarium? The Government told the Lok Sabha on 1 August 2025 that it had no proposal to raise the honorarium of Anganwadi workers and helpers, which was Rs 4,500 a month for a worker at a regular centre and Rs 2,250 for a helper, as last revised in October 2018. Any change would first have to appear in the allocations.

**3. Employment.** How much is provided for the rural employment guarantee, for the Employment Linked Incentive scheme and for skill programmes? In December 2025, a new law on rural employment replaced the MGNREGA framework, with a guarantee of 125 days of work, so the allocation for it will show how seriously the new framework is funded. The ELI scheme, approved in July 2025 with an outlay of Rs 99,446 crore, runs for jobs created between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027, so its yearly provision shows whether the target of more than 3.5 crore jobs is on track.

**4. Tax.** Is there relief for salaried workers and pensioners? Workers feel the effect of income tax and of indirect taxes on goods of daily use, and relief for those with fixed incomes is one of the most common requests in pre-Budget meetings.

**5. Micro and small industries.** Is credit available to the sector that employs more people than any other outside agriculture? Small enterprises hire most new workers, take most apprentices, and are also the first to be hurt by delayed payments and costly credit.

## How BMS approaches the Budget

In the pre-Budget consultations with the Finance Minister, BMS puts forward its suggestions. After the Budget, the Kendriya Karya Samiti or the national leadership usually issues a statement that welcomes what helps workers and points out what does not. The demands it has recently placed before the Government give a fair idea of its checklist. In its memorandum to the Labour Minister of 21 November 2025, BMS asked that the EPF wage ceiling be raised from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000, the ESI limit from Rs 21,000 to Rs 42,000, and the ceiling for calculating bonus from Rs 7,000 to Rs 14,000. It asked that the minimum pension be raised from Rs 1,000 to Rs 7,500, and that honoraria for Anganwadi, ASHA and mid-day meal workers be increased. It asked for a focus on labour-intensive sectors such as beedi, plantation, construction, handlooms, agriculture and fisheries, and for budgetary compensation for welfare boards, such as the beedi board, whose cess-based funding was removed after the introduction of GST. Most of these are Budget questions, since each one has a price.

## Reading the fine print

A good reading goes beyond the speech. Several things deserve attention:

- **Allocation against actual spending.** A scheme can be announced with a large number, and then spend less. The Budget documents show a "budget estimate", a "revised estimate" and "actuals" for earlier years, and the gap between them tells the real story.
- **New announcement or old money relabelled.** Sometimes an item shown as new is a continuation of an existing scheme under a new name.
- **Who actually receives the money.** An incentive paid through a bank account to the worker is different from one paid to an intermediary.
- **Timing.** A scheme that begins late in the year spends less in the year in which it is announced.
- **State share.** Many programmes need a contribution from State governments, which affects whether the money reaches the worker.

## Why the Budget and the Codes belong together

The Labour Codes set the rules, but the Budget decides which of them can be carried out in practice. Registration of unorganised and gig workers, a national floor wage, inspection aimed at helping compliance, and social security for lakhs of new beneficiaries all need administrative capacity and money. If the Codes are the structure, the Budget is the material with which it is built. A worker who has been told that the law has been improved is right to ask whether the Budget has paid for it.

## A few things to remember on Budget day

- The first reaction in the media is rarely the last word. Detailed documents are published after the speech, and the analysis that matters comes in the following days.
- Official statements, union statements and independent analyses will differ. It is wise to read more than one.
- A single figure for "social sector" or "employment" may combine many items, so one should look for the specific scheme.

## A closing thought

A Budget is read in crores, but it is felt in rupees: the honorarium that arrives on the first of the month, the health card that is accepted at the hospital, the pension that is a little higher, the loan that a small factory can get. Asking five plain questions is a simple way for any worker to judge it. BMS will, as it has done in earlier years, assess the Budget on that basis after it is presented, welcoming what helps workers and stating plainly what does not.
